description: The Vedic Age is the period in Indian history following the decline of the Indus Valley Civilization, shaped by the Indo-Aryans. Our primary sources of information for this rural and agrarian civilization are the Vedas and associated Vedic literature.

sections.title: Division and Sources of the Vedic Age
sections.description: The Vedic Age is divided into two distinct phases for historical study, with the Vedas serving as the foundational texts.

historical_events.significance: The Rigveda is the sole source of information for this period. The Aryans primarily settled in the Sapta Sindhu (Land of Seven Rivers) region.
Marked by the composition of the Samaveda, Yajurveda, and Atharvaveda, along with the Brahmanas, Aranyakas, and Upanishads.

key_concepts.explanation: Meaning 'that which has been heard'. These are sacred texts considered to be divine revelations passed down orally from generation to generation, encompassing the four Vedas.

Six auxiliary disciplines developed for the understanding and preservation of the Vedas: Shiksha (Phonetics), Kalpa (Ritual), Vyakarana (Grammar), Nirukta (Etymology), Chhanda (Meter), and Jyotisha (Astronomy).

key_associations.extra_info: The oldest Veda; consists of 10 Mandalas (books) and 1028 Suktas (hymns) dedicated to various deities.
Contains hymns sung during sacrifices; considered the foundational text for Indian classical music.
Deals with the rules, procedures, and formulas of sacrifices; uniquely written in both prose and poetry.
Contains spells, charms, magic, and information on ancient Indian medicine (Ayurveda).

sections.title: Geographical Expansion
sections.description: Details the territorial spread of the Aryans and the ancient names of vital river systems.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: The early settlement region of the Rigvedic Aryans, comprising the Indus River and its tributaries.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: Between the Saraswati and Drishadvati rivers
geographical_data.key_characteristics: Considered the most sacred geographical region by the Rigvedic Aryans.

geographical_data.location_or_origin: From the Himalayas to the Vindhya Mountains
geographical_data.key_characteristics: Represents the total geographical expansion of the Aryans into the Ganga-Yamuna Doab during the Later Vedic Period.

key_associations.extra_info: Ancient name of a major river in the Rigvedic text.
The famous 'Battle of Ten Kings' (Dasharajna Yuddha) was fought on the banks of this river.
A prominent river of the Sapta Sindhu region.
The easternmost river mentioned in the Rigvedic core region.

sections.title: Political and Social System
sections.description: The administrative framework, tribal organization, and societal structure during the Vedic era.

key_concepts.explanation: The chief or king of a tribe (Jana). During the Rigvedic period, the position was not purely hereditary, and the king's powers were highly restricted by tribal councils.
Democratic tribal assemblies that exercised control over the king. The 'Sabha' was an exclusive council of elders and elites, while the 'Samiti' was a general assembly of the entire tribe.
An occupation-based societal division first mentioned in the Purusha Sukta of the 10th Mandala of the Rigveda. It divided society into Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras.

important_facts.fact: The smallest unit of Vedic society was the family (Kula), headed by the eldest male member called 'Kulapa', reflecting a strongly patriarchal society.
During the Later Vedic Period, the Varna System became rigidly birth-based rather than occupation-based.
The position of women was respectable in the Early Vedic Period; widow remarriage and the Niyoga system were permitted, while child marriage and the Sati system were entirely absent.

sections.title: Economic and Religious Life
sections.description: The foundation of the Vedic economy, technological advancements, and the evolution of deities.

key_concepts.explanation: Literally translating to 'search for cows', this term was used for wars or conflicts. The cow was considered 'Aghanya' (not to be killed) and was the primary measure of wealth.
Refers to Iron, discovered around 1000 BCE during the Later Vedic Period. Its discovery revolutionized agriculture (iron plows) and warfare (weaponry).
In the Rigvedic period, it was a voluntary offering or gift made by the people to the king. In the Later Vedic Period, it became a mandatory, structured tax.

key_associations.extra_info: The most important deity of the Rigvedic period, with 250 hymns dedicated to him. He was the god of rain and thunder.
The second most important deity (200 hymns); acted as an intermediary between humans and gods through sacrificial fire.
Rose to prominence in the Later Vedic Period, replacing Indra as the most supreme deity.

sections.title: Important Philosophies and Facts
sections.description: Crucial philosophical schools (Shaddarshana), Upanishadic origins, and frequent exam-oriented one-liners.

key_associations.extra_info: The oldest school of Indian philosophy; emphasizes a dualistic reality of Purusha (consciousness) and Prakriti (matter).
Focuses on meditation, physical discipline, and spiritual liberation.
A school of philosophy dealing heavily with logic, epistemology, and analytical thinking.
Meaning 'the end of the Vedas', it forms the philosophical foundation based heavily on the teachings of the Upanishads.

important_facts.fact: India's national motto 'Satyameva Jayate' (Truth alone triumphs) is taken from the Mundaka Upanishad.
The famous 'Gayatri Mantra', dedicated to the solar deity Savitri, was composed by sage Vishvamitra and is found in the 3rd Mandala of the Rigveda.
The four Ashramas (stages of life) - Brahmacharya (Student), Grihastha (Householder), Vanaprastha (Retiree), and Sannyasa (Renunciate) - are first collectively mentioned in the Jabalopanishad.
